'''Gérard Nissim Amzallag''' ({{Langx|he|ז'ראר ניסים אמזלג}}) is a [[French people|French]]-[[Israel]]i biologist, born in Morocco in 1962. He is an associate researcher at [[Ben Gurion University]].<ref>{{Citation |chapter=Yahweh and the Origins of Ancient Israel |date=2023 |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/yahweh-and-the-origins-of-ancient-israel/yahweh-and-the-origins-of-ancient-israel/2E339CD23A7B1D74DFCFEE92A57BA792 |title=Yahweh and the Origins of Ancient Israel: Insights from the Archaeological Record |pages=i–ii |editor-last=Amzallag |editor-first=Nissim |access-date=2023-10-19 |place=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-009-31477-0}}</ref> He holds a doctorate in biblical studies.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2021-01-24 |title=" Le judaïsme n'a pas inventé le dieu de la Bible, mais transformé un culte secret en religion officielle " |language=fr |work=Le Monde.fr |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/le-monde-des-religions/article/2021/01/24/le-judaisme-n-a-pas-invente-le-dieu-de-la-bible-mais-transforme-un-culte-secret-en-religion-officielle_6067390_6038514.html |access-date=2023-10-19}}</ref> His work on the origins of [[Yahwism]] was controversially received, describing Yahweh's proposed origin as the [[Canaanite pantheon|Canaanite]] god of metallurgy.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Jewish God Yahweh Originated in Canaanite Vulcan, Says New Theory |language=en |work=Haaretz |url=https://www.haaretz.com/archaeology/2018-04-11/ty-article-magazine/.premium/jewish-god-yahweh-originated-in-canaanite-vulcan-says-new-theory/0000017f-dc86-d3ff-a7ff-fda6aa390000 |access-date=2023-10-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schlimm |first=Matthew Richard |date=2017 |title=Jealousy or Furnace Remelting?: A Response to Nissim Amzallag |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1353/jbl.2017.0033 |journal=Journal of Biblical Literature |volume=136 |issue=3 |pages=513–528 |doi=10.1353/jbl.2017.0033 |s2cid=149086612 |issn=1934-3876|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He has written on the origins of [[biblical archeology]] locations such as [[Edom]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Crowell |first=Bradley L. |title=Edom at the edge of empire: a social and political history |date=2021 |publisher=SBL Press |isbn=978-0-88414-528-8 |series=Archaeology and biblical studies |location=Atlanta, GA}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tebes |first=Juan Manuel |date=2019 |title=Memories of humiliation, cultures of resentment towards Edom and the formation of ancient Jewish national identity |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nana.12367 |journal=Nations and Nationalism |language=en |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=124–145 |doi=10.1111/nana.12367 |issn=1354-5078|hdl=11336/46149 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> and analyses of the [[Psalms]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schweers |first=Katherine |date=2023 |title=Uncovering Hidden Anger in the Psalms Using Psychological Models of Anger |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/01461079231191555 |journal=Biblical Theology Bulletin: Journal of Bible and Culture |language=en |volume=53 |issue=3 |pages=159–171 |doi=10.1177/01461079231191555 |s2cid=261431537 |issn=0146-1079|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His work on [[Yahweh]] and the [[Origins of Judaism]] has been cited by [[Daniel E. Fleming]]<ref>{{Citation |chapter=The Name Yahweh |date=2020-12-03 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1017/9781108875479.006 |title=Yahweh before Israel |pages=162–184 |access-date=2023-10-19 |publisher=Cambridge University Press|doi=10.1017/9781108875479.006 |isbn=9781108875479 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> and [[Yigal Levin]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Levin |first=Yigal |date=2020 |title=The Religion of Idumea and Its Relationship to Early Judaism |journal=Religions |language=en |volume=11 |issue=10 |pages=487 |doi=10.3390/rel11100487 |issn=2077-1444 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

It was also cited by detractors in 2010, "A Chalcolithic Error." Thornton et al named the academic as author of methodological and referential shortcomings, and "errata" too numerous to exhaust. The discussion (''sive'' conclusion) rounds up:

<blockquote>
Crucible and furnace
smelting methods are not... as different as the
author suggests, and we have provided... evidence for
the indigenous development of furnace technology
from earlier crucible smelting technologies. Contrary
to Amzallag's vision of advanced furnace smelting
originating in the southern Levant, we have demonstrated (it was a)
conservative area as far as smelting is concerned.
<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Thornton |first1=C.P. |last2=Golden |first2=J.M. |last3=Killick |first3=D.J. |last4=Pigott |first4=V.C. |last5=Rehren |first5=T.H. |last6=Roberts |first6=B.W. |date=2010 |title=A Chalcolithic Error: Rebuttal to Amzallag 2009 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25684276 |journal=American Journal of Archaeology |language=en |volume=114 |issue=2 |pages=305–315 |doi=10.3764/aja.114.2.305 |jstor=25684276 |issn=0002-9114}}</ref>

</blockquote>
This criticism didn't stop his output, however. In 2023, he published ''Yahweh and the Origins of Ancient Israel,'' moving forward based on previous musings on the metallurgical aspects of Yahweh. The author's multidisciplinary view is of a mainly volcanic and smithing [[Kenite hypothesis]] of Yahweh.<ref>{{Cite web |title=YHWH: The Kenite God of Metallurgy - TheTorah.com |url=https://www.thetorah.com/article/yhwh-the-kenite-god-of-metallurgy |access-date=2024-11-02 |website=www.thetorah.com}}</ref>
